title: 9. Both Sides of the Aisle, Likely Outcomes & No-FOMO Action Plan

epigraph.quote: Underwriting Rule: a great business is a reason to do the work, not a reason to pay any price.
epigraph.author: Research Desk house maxim

web_blocks.html: The locked decision. Pass 1 closed on a business-quality verdict of COMPOUNDER_PASS with KPI health PASS_WITH_WATCH. Pass 2 now prices that business, and the answer is different. Our new-capital verdict is WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT, conviction TIER_2 (archetype QUALITY_COMPOUNDER_STAGE3_PULLBACK, strategy bucket CORE_ALPHA). We allocate zero at the current price. The portfolio holds no MPS shares (NOT_HELD, 0 shares), so the decision concerns new capital only. The reasoning is short. At the verified ledger close of ₹2,297.00 on 12 November 2026, the probability-weighted 12-month value is ₹2,440 on our central earnings basis, a gain of only 6.2%. On the stricter basis it is ₹2,254, a loss of 1.9%. The reward-to-risk against our ₹2,005 invalidation level is 0.39:1 on the central basis, far under our 1.5:1 hurdle. On the stricter basis it is negative. From ₹2,150, the top of the support zone, the central ratio is 1.79:1 and the stricter ratio is 0.63:1. From ₹2,070, the bottom, they are 5.23:1 and 2.63:1. The later 13 November print of ₹2,259.30 comes from the TradingView pull after the NSE close and is not yet ledger-verified. It improves the central ratio only to 0.59:1. Under the snapshot’s stricter classifier the stock has already slipped to Stage 4, because it sits 0.12% under its 30-week average. So the stock is at the Stage 3/4 boundary. The business passes, and the price and timing do not yet. The rest of this chapter puts the strongest bull and bear arguments side by side, shows the scenario arithmetic on both earnings bases and sets the evidence gates. It then sizes the position we would take if the price came to us.

web_blocks.caption: Bull vs Bear: nine pillars, steelmanned on each side, with our independent judgment
web_blocks.takeaway: The bull case wins the debate on business quality: franchise and cash conversion. Concentration is improving but still elevated. The bear case wins on the three things that decide the price over the next year. Those are AI price give-back at renewal, the quality of acquired assets and the tape. Valuation is a draw. At 22.7x trailing earnings the stock sits on the five-year median and near the 75th percentile (23.0x) of the ten-year band. That band has a median of 17.6x, a 25th percentile of 13.8x and a maximum of 41.7x. So the multiple is reasonable, not a bargain. Probabilities in the last column are desk estimates, not company guidance. They are consistent with the odds stated in Chapters 4 and 5.
rows: Franchise and moat

A 56-year-old production and platform franchise embedded in the workflows of the largest scholarly and education publishers. Customers now buy three and four lines of work where they once bought one; the average count of MPS business units inside a star account rose from 2.5 to 5.5 over two years; ten-year operating cash flow roughly equals ten-year profit and ROCE has stayed in the mid-30s to high-30s since FY23 [2, 18, 1].

Our own moat scorecard averages about 3 out of 5: relationships and Unbound retention score 4, but certifications, “AI-first” and labour cost score 2 to 3, and every competitor from Straive to codemantra sells the same AI pitch. Springer Nature built nonsense-text and image detectors in house and donated one to the STM Integrity Hub, so detection alone can be pulled in-house [29, 61, 58].
Bull wins, about 70%: the franchise keeps earning above its cost of capital through 2030. It is a respectable moat built on relationships and platforms, not a wide technological one.
AI price deflation

Research EBITDA margin rose from 36.8% (FY25) to 39.9% (FY26) and then to 45.1% and 48.2% in Q1 and Q2 FY27 while Research employee cost fell 13.4% in FY26. The CEO’s framing is that customers share the productivity gain but MPS recovers it through volume, and management says 25% of revenue is now outcome-based [1, 25, 2].

RWS shows what the early damage looks like: FY25 revenue fell 4% while adjusted pre-tax profit fell from £106.7m to £60.4m. MPS’s own FY20 saw book-production prices cut about 20% on average. The large mandates have not yet been renewed under AI-era pricing, the 25% outcome-based share has no published definition, and FY26 outsourcing cost grew 9.7% against revenue growth of 5.7% [67, 12, 1].

Bear wins on direction, bull on level for the next four quarters. We put the weak form (continued deflation, MPS running to stand still) at about 80% and the strong form (margin below FY25’s 29.0% group level within three years) at about 20%; Research margin staying above 40% is about 70% and holding within three points of 48.2% only about 35%. This is the hinge of the whole case.
Customer concentration

The largest customer fell from 18.6% to 17.3% of revenue and the top 15 from 61.1% to 58.0% (audited); top-five share fell to 46% from 51% in Q2 FY27, and clients billed roughly doubled to about 840 as Unbound’s institutional base arrived. Contracts typically run three to five years [1, 2].

58% of revenue comes from 15 customers and, on the standalone entity, three customers above 10% each (39.0% of standalone revenue). AJE’s B2B referral channel was “entirely dependent on one publisher”. Appen lost a 30% customer and saw its largest division fall 38% within a year [1, 10, 37].

Bear wins on level, bull on direction. Concentration improved over the last year. The largest customer fell from 18.6% to 17.3%, the top 15 from 61.1% to 58.0% and the top five from 51% to 46%. But the largest customer is still well above its FY23 level of 11.9%. One procurement decision can still move group margin. We put the chance of a top-three customer loss, a re-tender at lower rates, or a largest customer above 20% within 12 months at about 15%.
Corporate Learning

H1 FY27 EBITDA margin about 25% against about 16%, EBITDA up 77% with 19% fewer people, Q2 revenue up 17%; Liberate is now wholly owned and a new segment president is in place. A turn here would add earnings on a small base (12.5% of FY26 revenue) [2, 1].

FY26 revenue fell 16.5% and segment result fell from ₹20.00 Cr to ₹11.31 Cr. Management has missed three separate recovery dates; the corporate market grows 12% to 13% against MPS’s 6% to 7%; the segment head herself says “this is not a recovery of the legacy business”; and ₹100.38 Cr of goodwill sits against an ₹11.31 Cr segment result, 8.9 times [25, 19, 1].

Skeptic wins on the thesis, bull on the margin. Treat it as an option on a turnaround, not a pillar. We put the margin staying above 18% for the next four quarters at about 70%, and growth back near 12% by FY28 at about 35%.
Acquisitions and goodwill

Entry prices have been disciplined: Unbound at US$16.5 million was 2.09 times its annual revenue and 23.6 times its profit; AJE costing about ₹70 Cr “earns more than half of that back every year now”. The CEO: “I would rather miss a deal than overpay.” MPS is debt-free and says Unbound is “our new template” [1, 2].

Goodwill of ₹376.32 Cr is 40% of total assets and goodwill plus acquired intangibles 52.5%. AJE’s provisional goodwill was cut 28% in the measurement period; Liberate has already been impaired by ₹12.93 Cr; the Unbound allocation is provisional until February 2027 and 88% of its price is goodwill. Management promised “five deals lined up” and did one in twelve months [1, 17].

Bear wins on integration record, bull on price discipline. We put the chance of a goodwill impairment above ₹25 Cr in the next 12 months at about 10%, and treat a large new deal as a risk event, not a catalyst, until the first six months of its numbers are public.
Cash conversion and capital return

Operating cash flow over ten years is 1.00 times profit; capex is about 1.1% of revenue; FY26 free cash flow after leases was ₹23.89 per ₹100 of revenue; ₹651 Cr (about 99% of FY19 to FY25 profit) went back to shareholders; ₹163 Cr cash and no debt at 30 September 2026. The CEO: “the business is throwing out INR15 crores to INR18 crores of cash every month” [1, 25, 2].

FY25 operating cash flow was only 68% of profit; FY26’s 83% of EBITDA came in a year when working capital was neutral; about ₹14 Cr of FY26 pre-tax profit was exceptional gain or liability write-back; no FY26 final dividend was declared and the CEO says distributions resume only “once that capital is deployed”, so the current yield is nil [1, 2].
Bull wins, about 75% that free cash flow after leases stays above 80% of profit. But the payout record is a past fact, not a current cash yield, and a new acquisition delays it again.
Governance and the ADI BPO merger

The promoter holds 68.34% and has not sold; the amalgamation puts ADI BPO’s own shareholders directly on the MPS register; MPS says public shareholders are not diluted; the equity meeting approved it with all promoter and institutional votes and 1,52,327 of 1,52,377 non-institutional votes in favour; the CEO and CFO are the continuity [1, 11, 95].

One person is chairman and CEO and was paid 191 times the median employee in FY26, up 31.33%; the company secretary, the CFO and the Corporate Learning heads have changed; the audit-trail exception has repeated for three years; the court-convened vote was carried mainly by the promoter’s own 68%; and final sanction is unconfirmed [1, 96].
Slight bear until final sanction, about 80% that the scheme closes as described. The residual risks are overhang if new direct holders sell, and any change in terms; the latter is a cancel trigger.
Valuation

Enterprise value of ₹3,784 Cr is 13.6 times trailing EBITDA of ₹279 Cr and 12.0 times our FY27E EBITDA of ₹315 Cr. P/E on FY27E EPS of about ₹124.5 is 18.4 times, and the FCFF yield is 5.7%. The reverse DCF needs average FCF growth of about 8.8% a year along the fade path (12.6% in year one fading to 5%), at a 13% discount rate. EBITDA compounded 17.1% a year over FY21 to FY26. MPS has the highest ROCE and margin in its peer set [2, 1].

22.7x trailing earnings equals the five-year median and is near the 75th percentile of the ten-year band, so there is no discount to history. Year-one growth of 12.6% is implied at a 13% discount rate, above the ten-year EBITDA CAGR of 10.2%. Dividend yield is nil. On P/E, MPS (20.74) trades about 10% above Datamatics (18.87) and 6% above Newgen (19.6). It is well above NIIT Learning Systems (9.87). Its ROCE of 38.7% against peers’ 20.4% to 25.0% explains a premium, but the premium is already in the price.

A draw: fair, not cheap. It is a fair price for a high-quality business, not a margin of safety. At the 18x base multiple, central-basis EPS gives only +4.9% from ₹2,297.00. The stricter year-end basis gives -2.4%. At ₹2,150 the stock is on 17.3 times FY27E EPS and 11.2 times FY27E EBITDA, closer to the ten-year median.
Tape

The 200-day average is rising (₹2,069.06, up from ₹1,918.86 sixty-three sessions earlier); the stock gained 38% in six months; it has compounded 26.1% a year over five years; and all three listed peers (Datamatics, NIIT Learning Systems, Newgen) are in Stage 4 and down 18% to 56% over a year while MPS is roughly flat.

Close below a falling 50-day average (₹2,517 on the ledger, down from ₹2,704), RSI 42, nine distribution days in 25 sessions, volume at 0.36 times its 20-day average, relative strength of -26.7% over 28 days, a close 22.9% under the 52-week high, and a snapshot classification of Stage 4 with the timing gate rejected. Three drawdowns of 50% or more since 2015 (-57.7%, -67.5%, -51.9%).

Bear wins for the next one to three months, about 60/40. The 30-week average at ₹2,262 is the shelf: the 13 November close of ₹2,259.30 is sitting on it, and a weekly close below it would confirm Stage 4. We act on the rising 200-day average and the swing low, not on the shelf.

web_blocks.caption: 12-month scenario matrix, central earnings basis B (value date about November 2027; reference price ₹2,297.00 at the 12 November ledger close)
web_blocks.takeaway: On the central basis the probability-weighted value is ₹2,440, a gain of 6.2% from ₹2,297.00. The distribution is skewed the way a quality compounder’s should be: bull +44.1% against bear -29.1%. But half the weight sits on the base case, which pays only 4.9%. The multiples map to history. The 14x bear multiple is close to the ten-year 25th percentile (13.8x). The 18x base multiple matches the ten-year median (17.6x), and the 22x bull multiple matches the five-year median (22.7x). All scenarios assume D&A of ₹36 Cr in FY27E and ₹38 Cr in FY28E, other income of ₹8 Cr, interest of ₹3 Cr, tax of 25% and 1.7106 Cr shares. The 25/50/25 weights are a judgment. Moving to 35/45/20 would lower this weighted value to about ₹2,317. The verdict does not depend on the weights, because the decision rule is the reward-to-risk at the support zone.
rows: Bear

AI price give-back at a large renewal and a Corporate Learning stall. Research margin falls back to about 40%. An acquisition stumbles through an impairment or a late integration. FY27 lands on ₹300 Cr, slightly under the ₹310 Cr floor. The multiple compresses to the ten-year lower quartile.
Base

The FY27 floor of at least ₹310 Cr is delivered (our FY27E is ₹315 Cr). FY28 grows about 14% to ₹360 Cr, a group margin of about 33% to 34%. Unbound and the new Research mandates reach steady state. Research margin holds in the mid-40s. The multiple eases to the ten-year median.
Bull

One or two acquisitions on top of the organic base. Research margin near 50%, Education recovers and Corporate Learning grows. EBITDA approaches Vision 2027’s ₹450 Cr. The multiple holds at the five-year median.

web_blocks.caption: The same scenarios on two earnings bases (value date about November 2027; multiples 14x / 18x / 22x)
web_blocks.takeaway: The ten-year P/E band is built on last-reported fiscal-year EPS. At a November 2027 value date, the matching EPS on the band’s own basis is FY27E. That is basis A, the stress case. Basis B uses last-twelve-months EPS at the value date, the average of FY27E and FY28E. It is our central case, because markets price on current earnings and a lagging EPS understates what the market typically pays. Basis B is the more generous reading, and we do not call the two the same basis. On basis A the weighted value is slightly below today’s price. That is why the position is sized so that the verdict survives the stricter reading.
rows: A. Year-end EPS, the band’s own basis (FY27E EPS ₹117.9 / ₹124.5 / ₹131.1)
B. LTM EPS at the value date (₹116.4 / ₹133.9 / ₹150.4), central case

web_blocks.html: The EPS and multiple logic. Each scenario multiplies two numbers: what the business earns and what the market pays for a rupee of it. The multiples come from the ten-year band of P/E on last-reported fiscal-year EPS. We show two earnings bases. Basis A uses FY27E EPS of ₹117.9, ₹124.5 and ₹131.1. Basis B uses last-twelve-months EPS at the value date, taken as the average of FY27E and FY28E: ₹116.4, ₹133.9 and ₹150.4. FY26 EPS was ₹101.26 on the aggregator’s basis (₹102.11 audited basic). Our base-case LTM EPS of ₹133.9 is 32.2% above that. The driver is the guided FY27 EBITDA floor of at least ₹310 Cr, raised from ₹300 Cr on 4 November 2026. H1 FY27 EBITDA was already ₹154 Cr. On top of that floor we assume about 14% growth in FY28 [2]. That growth rate is below the 17.1% EBITDA CAGR of FY21 to FY26 and above the 10.2% ten-year CAGR, a deliberate middle. The base multiple of 18x is lower than today’s 22.7x trailing. We ask the market to pay less per rupee of earnings, and the result is a base return of only 4.9% on basis B and -2.4% on basis A. The bear value of ₹1,630 is 24.2% below the ₹2,150 entry zone. That matters for sizing, because our ₹2,005 daily-close stop is a risk-control level, not a worst case.

web_blocks.caption: Why the price matters: the same scenario values against four entry prices (stop ₹2,005 on a daily close; base target ₹2,410 on basis B and ₹2,241 on basis A)
web_blocks.takeaway: At the ₹2,297.00 ledger close the stock offers ₹113 of upside to the central base case against ₹292 of risk to the stop. That is 0.39:1, far below our 1.5:1 hurdle. On basis A the base value is below the price, so the ratio is negative. The 13 November print of ₹2,259.30 gives 0.59:1 on basis B and -0.07:1 on basis A. The ₹2,070 tranche clears 1.5:1 on both bases, at 5.23:1 and 2.63:1. It is the core order. The ₹2,150 tranche clears 1.5:1 only on basis B, at 1.79:1. On basis A it is 0.63:1. The ₹2,150 tranche needs a base value of at least ₹2,367.50. Basis B clears that by 1.8%, and basis A misses it by ₹126.5. So the ₹2,150 tranche is conditional. An expected return of +6.2% on the central basis is about half of what a 13% cost of equity demands. You are not paid for the risk.

web_blocks.html: Why a limit buy is consistent with a Stage 4 reading. We take the stricter Stage 4 reading to forbid buying at the current price or on a bounce. The limit buys at ₹2,070 and ₹2,150 are a different, deliberate trade. They are a half-size, counter-trend support entry at the rising 200-day average (₹2,069), inside a long-term uptrend. That average still slopes up and was ₹1,919 sixty-three sessions ago. The ₹2,070 order sits right on that average and clears our reward-to-risk hurdle on both earnings bases (2.63:1 and 5.23:1). It is the order most consistent with the Stage 4 reading. The ₹2,150 order clears the hurdle only on the central basis (1.79:1), so it is conditional. We abandon both orders if the daily close breaks ₹2,005. This is not a Stage 2 entry, and it does not claim that the trend has turned.

Independent verdict across three horizons.
1. Short term (1 to 3 months): WAIT. The tape is at the Stage 3/4 boundary. The close of ₹2,297 on 12 November (₹2,259.30 on 13 November) is under a falling 50-day average of about ₹2,500 to ₹2,517. There are nine distribution days in 25 sessions and RSI is between 40 and 42. A weekly close under the 30-week shelf of ₹2,262 would confirm Stage 4. We see no edge in front-running either direction. The next evidence is the Q3 FY27 print and the Unbound allocation, due by February 2027 [1].
2. Medium term (6 to 18 months): ACCUMULATE only inside ₹2,070 to ₹2,150 with the ₹2,005 daily-close stop, or after a confirmed re-base and a fresh re-underwrite, provided the evidence gates hold. The core order is two-thirds of the starter at ₹2,070. The one-third at ₹2,150 is conditional: we place it only if the re-derived base value is at or above ₹2,367.50 on basis A. H2 FY27 EBITDA must be at least ₹156 Cr, so that FY27 reaches the ₹310 Cr floor after H1’s ₹154 Cr. Our base case needs about ₹161 Cr. Research EBITDA margin must stay at or above 45% and Corporate Learning margin above 18%. There must be no goodwill impairment above ₹25 Cr. The largest customer should stay at or below about 17% and the top-five share at or below 46%. A re-base means a weekly close above the 30-week average with the 10-week EMA (₹2,416 on the 13 November print) turning up on rising volume. A weekly close above the falling 50-day average near ₹2,500 with the 30-week average rising also re-opens the file. Neither is an automatic add.
3. Long term (3 to 5 years): a genuine compounder candidate (COMPOUNDER_PASS). The business-quality case is intact. Ten-year operating cash flow equals profit, capex is about 1% of revenue and the balance sheet is debt-free. The debate for this horizon is price, AI price give-back and acquisition discipline, not whether the franchise exists. Three prior 50%-plus drawdowns tell us the entry price decides whether a five-year holding feels like a compounder or a roller coaster.

web_blocks.caption: What would change our mind: upgrade triggers and cancel triggers
web_blocks.takeaway: Upgrade triggers are about confirmation, and none of them is an automatic add. Each one re-opens the file for a fresh re-underwrite. Any add must clear 1.5:1 from the add price to a re-based stop. One business trigger also activates the conditional ₹2,150 tranche. Cancel triggers are business-level and apply regardless of price. Any one of them removes MPS from the watch even if the stock reaches the support zone. They would break the Pass 1 case rather than reprice it. The ₹2,005 daily close is the only price-based cancel.

web_blocks.html: What we might be wrong about. The hinge claim of this chapter is that Research margin durability survives the AI price give-back at the next large renewal. Research is 60% of revenue and about two-thirds of segment profit. Its margin has risen from 36.8% in FY25 to 48.2% in Q2 FY27. The CEO’s own account is that customers “expect to share in our productivity” [1, 2]. The base case assumes the sharing is real but affordable, so price falls and volume rises by more. It needs Research margin in the mid-40s through the next AI-era re-bid. Suppose instead the first large re-bid resets unit rates by 15% to 20% with no matching volume commitment. That is the size of the FY20 offshore book-production cut. Research margin would then drop toward 40% within two quarters. The bear case’s ₹295 Cr FY28E EBITDA would be a reasonable outcome, and a purchase at ₹2,150 would have been made for the wrong reason. The margin does not need to fall that far to hurt. Two quarters under about 41% to 42% would hurt. So would a lower-rate re-tender of the 17.3% customer. A 20% re-tender of that customer is about ₹26.6 Cr of revenue. Flowing fully to EBITDA for a year, it takes the base value to about ₹2,306. For half a year it takes it to about ₹2,358. Both figures are on basis B, and both are below the ₹2,367.50 line for the ₹2,150 tranche. The error in the other direction is also real. The stock has already pulled back 22.9% from its high. If it reclaims ₹2,500 on volume without visiting ₹2,150, we forgo roughly the first 10% of that move. We accept that. At ₹2,500 our current base value of ₹2,410 would give a negative reward. A missed 10% costs no capital, while a bear-case ₹1,630 costs 24.2% from the top of the zone. Two further things could make this analysis wrong. Our P/E mapping assumes historical multiples are a sane guide for a business moving toward subscriptions and outcome-based pricing. If the market starts to treat MPS as a software-like compounder, 22x will look cheap and 14x will look absurd. And the half-size rule assumes thin liquidity and gap risk matter for a ₹1.4 lakh position. They do for exits but not for entries.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Passing the business is not the same as buying the stock
paragraphs: Five chapters of the audit said yes. Cash matches profit, capex is near 1% of revenue, the balance sheet has no debt, and margins rose through an AI shift. It is tempting to let that momentum carry the decision. The discipline of this chapter is to separate two questions that a rising price blurs together. Is this a good business, and is this a good price for it? The first answer is yes, with real conditions. The second is “not yet, and here is the price at which it becomes yes”.

A 6.2% expected return at 0.39:1 is not an ordinary bet. It is a poor one. On the stricter earnings basis the expected return is negative. Such a bet in a stock that fell 51.9% and then rose 110.5% inside two years does not deserve an allocation. Waiting for ₹2,070, and only conditionally ₹2,150, is not pessimism about MPS. It is respect for how violently this particular stock has been priced.

web_blocks.intro: Position sizing decides how much of your capital rides on one idea, so that a wrong call costs a planned amount and not a surprise. Tier TIER_2 carries a range of 4% to 6.5% of net worth and a risk budget of 75 bps of net worth. On net worth of ₹42,91,664 that budget is ₹32,187. At an entry of ₹2,150 and a stop of ₹2,005, the stop sits 6.74% below entry (₹145 a share). The raw risk-unit weight is 0.75% divided by 6.74%, or 11.1%. The tier cap limits it to 6.5% (₹2,78,958). Our rule for MPS is a starter of about half the cap, 3.25% of net worth (₹1,39,479), in two tranches. The core order is two-thirds of the starter, about 2.17% (₹92,986), at ₹2,070. It clears 1.5:1 on both earnings bases. The conditional order is one-third, about 1.08% (₹46,493), at ₹2,150. It clears 1.5:1 only on the central basis. We place it only if, on the day, the re-derived base value is at or above ₹2,367.50 on basis A. That needs FY27E EPS of about ₹131.5, or FY27 EBITDA of roughly ₹331 Cr or more. Otherwise we skip it and keep the cash. If it is skipped, the first fill is about 2.17% of net worth, not 3.25%. Three facts drive the half-size rule. The stock has had three drawdowns of 50% or more since 2015 (-57.7%, -67.5% and -51.9% on weekly closes). Liquidity is thin at roughly 15,000 to 19,000 shares a day. And a 6.74% stop is gap-prone in a stock like this. We release the rest of the cap only after a confirmed re-base and a fresh re-underwrite that clears 1.5:1. The compiler’s execution table that follows shows 0.0% and 0 bps today. That is because the verdict is WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT, so there is no live allocation until the price is in the zone. The 75 bps risk budget and the 6.5% cap apply once a tranche is triggered.

web_blocks.html: Rupee examples on net worth of ₹42,91,664. In whole shares, the core order at ₹2,070 buys 44 shares for ₹91,080 (2.12% of net worth). The conditional order at ₹2,150 buys 21 shares for ₹45,150 (1.05%). If both fill, that is 65 shares costing ₹1,36,230 (3.17% of net worth) at a blended ₹2,095.85. If only the core order fills, the first fill is ₹91,080. If the stock closes through ₹2,005 and we exit there, the loss is ₹5,905 with both orders and ₹2,860 with the core order alone. That is 0.14% and 0.07% of net worth, well inside the 75 bps budget. We also test the sizing against the bear case, not just the stop. If the stock fell to the bear value of ₹1,630, the full starter would lose about ₹30,280 (0.71% of net worth), just inside the budget. The core order alone would lose about ₹19,360 (0.45%). A full 6.5% position filled at ₹2,150 is 129 shares (₹2,77,350). It would lose about ₹67,080 (1.56% of net worth) at ₹1,630, more than twice the budget. At the full cap the loss to the stop alone is ₹18,705 (0.44%), which is inside the budget. It is gap risk, not the stop, that argues for half size. Liquidity. Median daily volume is about 14,680 shares over the last 20 sessions and about 17,615 over the last 250. Median daily traded value is about ₹3.6 Cr. Our 65 shares are about 0.4% of one median day’s volume and of one day’s value, so entry will not move the price. The exit is the problem. Volume was 6,719 shares on 12 November (0.36 times its 20-day average) and 7,306 on 13 November. A stop at ₹2,005 is a trigger, not a guarantee of that price. We treat it as an alert and review it daily instead of relying on an automatic order. Cash. Cash is ₹5,74,582 (13.4% of net worth). The full starter leaves about ₹4,38,352 (10.2%). The core order alone leaves about ₹4,83,502 (11.3%). Cash covers the full starter about 4.2 times and even the full 6.5% cap about 2.1 times.

Corporate-structure watch item: the ADI BPO amalgamation. ADI BPO Services Ltd, the promoter holding company, owns 1,16,90,615 of MPS’s 1,71,05,816 shares (68.34%). The board approved the amalgamation of ADI BPO into MPS on 18 July 2025. The equity shareholders approved it on 22 August 2026. The NCLT Chennai second-motion order is dated 16 September 2026, and a further hearing was listed for 4 November 2026 [97, 96]. We could not find the outcome of that hearing, so final sanction is unconfirmed. A trade-press headline reading “NCLT approves” refers to the 16 September order. That order directed notices to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, the Registrar of Companies, tax authorities and the Official Liquidator, with 30 days for representations. It is a procedural step, not the final sanction [96, 98]. MPS describes the mechanics this way. ADI BPO first demerges its infrastructure-management business into ADI Holdings Pvt Ltd. It then merges into MPS and dissolves without winding up. ADI BPO’s 68.34% holding in MPS is cancelled, and the same number of MPS shares is issued to ADI BPO’s own shareholders on a share exchange ratio. There is no cash consideration, and the scheme is designed to be tax-neutral [95, 98]. If those statements hold, the public stays at 54,15,201 shares, 31.66% of the register.

web_blocks.caption: ADI BPO amalgamation: what to verify before the item is closed
web_blocks.takeaway: Nothing in the record we read suggests a loss for public shareholders. The near-unanimous non-institutional vote (1,52,327 for, 50 against) is consistent with that. But four checks remain open. The one with a price consequence is the overhang. 1% of MPS is 1,71,058 shares, about 11.7 days of median volume or about ₹39 Cr at ₹2,297. A change in terms is a cancel trigger.

web_blocks.html: How to read the panels that follow. The holding-action, alerts and redeployment panels rendered after this chapter apply the decision above. The holding action is NOT_HELD with 0 shares, so there is nothing to sell. The limit-zone alerts are ₹2,070, the core order for two-thirds of the starter, and ₹2,150, a conditional order for one-third. We place the ₹2,150 order only if the re-derived base value is at or above ₹2,367.50 on basis A. The cancel alert fires on a daily close below ₹2,005. The upgrade alert is a weekly close above about ₹2,500. It means re-underwrite, not add. The redeployment panel earmarks 100% of the reviewed capital as cash for MPS support-zone entries. It gives 0% to AJMERA, an existing 4.06%-weight holding with its own dossier whose sizing is a portfolio-audit decision, not funded here. It gives 0% to outside peers, because Datamatics, NIIT Learning Systems and Newgen are all Stage 4 and rejected by the timing gate. The panels are recommendations and alerts for you to act on, not standing orders. MPS is not in the NSE futures-and-options segment, so cash equity is the only instrument.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Cash is a position
paragraphs: When the plan says “wait”, it is tempting to read it as inaction. It is not. A 13.4% cash balance with a named place to go is an active position. ₹5,74,582 is earmarked for a stock we like, at a price we have computed, with a cancel level and a list of things that would change our mind. The alternative is buying a half-position now because the business is good and the stock is down 22.9%. The numbers have not asked for that position.

The discipline also protects against the opposite mistake. Suppose the stock never returns to ₹2,070 and instead reclaims ₹2,500 on volume. The upgrade trigger then re-opens the file. It does not tell us to buy. Missing a 10% rally is cheap. Owning a bear-case ₹1,630 position at full size is not.

web_blocks.html: Re-underwrite triggers (upgrade): move from WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT to a first fill only when the stock trades inside ₹2,070 to ₹2,150, the ₹2,005 stop is intact on a daily close and no business-level cancel trigger is active. The core order is two-thirds of the starter at ₹2,070. The one-third order at ₹2,150 is conditional. We place it only if the re-derived base value, re-run with the latest quarter’s results and guidance, is at or above ₹2,367.50 on basis A. That needs FY27 EBITDA of roughly ₹331 Cr or more. Otherwise we skip it and keep the cash. A weekly close above the falling 50-day average near ₹2,500 with the 30-week average rising is not an automatic add. It does not release the rest of the 6.5% cap. It re-opens the file for a fresh re-underwrite. We re-derive the base value from the latest results, because the current ₹2,410 central base is below ₹2,500. We re-base the stop to the new base and the 200-day average. Any add must clear 1.5:1 from the add price to the new stop. The same test applies after a weekly close above the 30-week average with the 10-week EMA turning up. We also want H2 FY27 EBITDA tracking at least ₹156 Cr (FY27 at or above the ₹310 Cr floor), Research margin at or above 45%, Corporate Learning margin above 18% and the ADI BPO scheme sanctioned without dilution. Cancel the watch on any of these. A daily close below ₹2,005. Research margin below 42% for two quarters. A largest customer above 20%, or a top-three customer loss. Corporate Learning margin back below 18% for two quarters. Any goodwill impairment above ₹25 Cr. An FY27 EBITDA guidance cut below ₹300 Cr. ADI BPO terms changing to be dilutive to public holders.

book_paragraphs: Here is where we stop admiring the machine and decide what to do with it. Five chapters ago you and I opened the hood on MPS: a 56-year-old content-engineering franchise that sits inside the production line of the world’s biggest scholarly and education publishers, turns a rupee of cash flow into roughly a rupee of profit, spends about one percent of revenue on capital equipment, and is debt-free again. We called that a compounder. I still do. And yet the verdict I am handing you is to wait, with no allocation at today’s price.

Let me say that plainly, because it is the sort of sentence that sounds like hedging and is not. The business passes. The new-capital verdict is wait for support, conviction tier two, zero allocation at the current price. You do not hold the stock, so there is nothing to sell. What you hold is a decision about whether to spend new money, and I want to show you why the honest answer today is not yet, and what price and what evidence would turn that into a yes.

Start with the tape, because it is the part you can see. On the last verified session, 12 November, MPS closed at ₹2,297. The next day, in a later print we have not yet been able to verify with the exchange data, it closed at ₹2,259.30. Either way the stock is about twenty-three percent below its August high of ₹2,979, it is trading under a falling fifty-day average near ₹2,500, and it has just made nine distribution days in twenty-five sessions on thin volume. One of our two classifiers calls that Stage 3, a topping or pulling-back phase; the stricter one already calls it Stage 4 because the price is sitting just under its thirty-week average. The honest summary is that the stock is at the boundary between the two.

Now the price tag. Multiply our three outcomes by their odds: a bear case at ₹1,630 with a one-in-four chance, a base case at ₹2,410 with even odds, and a bull case at ₹3,310 with a one-in-four chance. You get a probability-weighted value of ₹2,440. That is only six percent above ₹2,297. And that is the generous reading. The multiples we use come from a history built on the last reported year of earnings. If you value the business on that same year-end basis, the weighted value is ₹2,254, a little below today’s price. I treat the first reading as the central case and the second as the stress test. Now think about what you are being asked to accept. If you buy at ₹2,297 and our stop at ₹2,005 is right, you risk ₹292 a share to make ₹113 to the base case. That is not a bet. If you buy at ₹2,150, the top of the support zone, you risk ₹145 to make ₹260 on the central reading, a ratio of 1.8 to 1. On the stress reading it is only 0.6 to 1. At ₹2,070 you risk ₹65 to make ₹340 on the central reading and ₹171 on the stress reading, which is still better than two and a half to one. Same business, same forecast; only the price changed.

I want to be a fair judge of both sides, so let me argue the bull case as well as I can. The best evidence for it is the margin story. Research, which is sixty percent of revenue, went from a 36.8% EBITDA margin in FY25 to 48.2% in the latest quarter, on a headcount that barely moved. Top-five customers fell to forty-six percent of revenue. The company has ₹163 crore of cash and no debt. The CEO told the Q1 FY27 call that “the business is throwing out INR15 crores to INR18 crores of cash every month”, and the audited accounts back that rhythm. If you want to believe in a quality compounder, that is what the evidence looks like.

And now the bear, which deserves equal respect. Every one of those margin gains has been earned while the customers have not yet renegotiated. The CEO said it himself on the same call: “Customers expect to share in our productivity, and they do, but we kind of make that up through more volume, and that’s where the margin kind of comes from.” Read that again. It says the customers will take some of the gain. The question is how much, and when. A translation-services group called RWS saw revenue fall four percent while its adjusted profit fell from £106.7 million to £60.4 million. That is what a price give-back looks like when it arrives: not in the top line, in the profit. MPS has not yet shown us a large renewal at AI-era prices. That is the hinge.

Add the acquisition ledger. Goodwill is ₹376 crore, forty percent of total assets. The AJE deal’s provisional goodwill was cut by twenty-eight percent when the auditors finished; Liberate has already been impaired; and the Unbound allocation will not be final until February 2027. In fairness, the CEO has said on the Q2 FY27 call, “I would rather miss a deal than overpay,” and the entry prices support him: Unbound cost about twice its annual revenue. But the record on integration is mixed, and a company that has talked about “five deals lined up” and done one has taught you something about its timelines.

So our independent judgment, in the order you will ask me for it. On franchise and cash conversion, the bull wins. On concentration, the bull wins the direction and the bear wins the level. On AI price give-back, acquired assets and the tape, the bear wins the argument for the next twelve months, though I put the strongest version of the bear case at only about twenty percent. On valuation, nobody wins: at 22.7 times trailing earnings the stock sits on its five-year median and near the top quarter of its ten-year range, which is fair, not cheap. Put those together and you get a good business at a fair price in a weak tape. That is a wait.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Passing the business is not the same as buying the stock
book_callouts.quote: A good business at a fair price is an ordinary bet; a good business at a low price is an extraordinary one.
book_callouts.text: After five chapters of evidence in favour, the pull is to let the audit decide the purchase. I try to keep two questions apart: is this a good business, and is this a good price. MPS passes the first with real conditions and does not yet pass the second. A six percent expected return at today’s price, against a risk more than twice the reward, is not worth taking. On the stricter reading it is a small loss. The place where I would feel paid for taking the risk is ₹2,070, and only conditionally ₹2,150.
bullets: Business quality: COMPOUNDER_PASS, with KPI health PASS_WITH_WATCH.
Price: ₹2,297 gives 0.39:1; ₹2,150 gives 1.79:1 (0.63:1 on the stress reading); ₹2,070 gives 5.23:1 (2.63:1).
Rule: pay for quality at a price that pays you for the risk.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Cash is a position
book_callouts.quote: Waiting is a decision with a price attached.
book_callouts.text: A thirteen-percent cash balance with a named destination, an alert zone and a cancel level is an active position, not an absence of one. The cost of waiting is that if the stock reclaims ₹2,500 on volume without visiting our zone, we lose the first ten percent of the move. Even then the upgrade alert only re-opens the file; it is not a buy signal. The cost of not waiting is a bear case that takes a quarter of the capital. I would take the first cost every time.
bullets: Limit zone: ₹2,070 (core, two-thirds of the starter) and ₹2,150 (conditional one-third); cancel on a daily close below ₹2,005.
Upgrade alert: a weekly close above about ₹2,500 means re-underwrite, not add.
Zero shares held today; 100% of reviewed capital stays in cash.

book_subsections.title: Three horizons and the evidence that would change our mind
paragraphs: Let me give you the timetable. For the next one to three months the answer is wait. There is no edge in guessing whether the stock lands on the thirty-week average, falls through it, or bounces; the next real evidence arrives with the Q3 FY27 results and the final allocation of the Unbound purchase price by February 2027.

Over six to eighteen months the answer is accumulate, but only on our terms. That means inside the zone of ₹2,070 to ₹2,150, with a stop at a daily close below ₹2,005. It also means starting small. The core order is two thirds of the starter at ₹2,070. The other third, at ₹2,150, is conditional on the freshly re-run base value being high enough. A weekly close above the thirty-week average, or above the falling fifty-day average near ₹2,500, does not trigger an add by itself. It re-opens the file, and any add has to clear one and a half to one on fresh numbers. And the business has to keep its side of the bargain: second-half EBITDA of at least ₹156 crore so the ₹310 crore guidance is reached, Research margin of at least forty-five percent, Corporate Learning margin above eighteen percent.

Over three to five years, this is the horizon where I would be happy to own it. A company that converts profit to cash this reliably, spends so little on capital and has the balance sheet to buy what it likes belongs on a long-term list. What decides whether that holding feels like compounding or like a roller coaster is the price you pay. This stock has fallen fifty-eight percent, sixty-seven percent and fifty-two percent in three separate stretches since 2015. I will not ask you to forget that.

And here is what would make me cancel the idea, regardless of price. If Research margin dropped below forty-two percent for two quarters, I would know the price give-back had arrived. If the biggest customer grew past twenty percent of revenue, or a top-three customer left or re-tendered at lower rates, I would stop. If Corporate Learning margin fell back under eighteen percent, if any goodwill write-down exceeded ₹25 crore, if the ₹310 crore guide were cut under ₹300 crore, or if the promoter merger changed terms to the public’s disadvantage, I would stop. These are not price alerts. They are breaks in the reasons we passed the business.

book_subsections.title: Sizing it like someone who has been surprised before
paragraphs: Now position size, because the first mistake investors make with a good idea is to size it like a certainty. Our rules put a stock of this conviction between four and six and a half percent of your net worth, with a risk budget of seventy-five basis points. On a net worth of ₹42,91,664, that budget is ₹32,187. At an entry of ₹2,150 and a stop of ₹2,005, your stop is 6.74 percent away, and the raw arithmetic says you could hold eleven percent of your net worth. The tier cap stops that at six and a half.

I want you to hold at most half of that cap, about three and a quarter percent, which is ₹1,39,479. And I want you to build it in two pieces. The core piece is two thirds, about two and a sixth percent of your net worth, at ₹2,070: 44 shares for ₹91,080. The other third, at ₹2,150, is conditional. It clears our reward-to-risk hurdle only on the generous earnings reading, so you place it only if the freshly re-run base value is at least ₹2,367.50 on the stricter reading. That needs FY27 EBITDA of roughly ₹331 crore or more. If not, you skip it and keep the cash. If both fill, that is 65 shares for ₹1,36,230. If the stock then closes below ₹2,005 and you leave, you lose ₹5,905, about fourteen hundredths of a percent of your net worth. If it falls all the way to our bear case of ₹1,630, the full starter loses about ₹30,280, just inside the whole risk budget, while a full-size position would lose more than twice that. That is why we start small.

Three facts drove the half-size. This stock has dropped more than fifty percent three times. It trades only fifteen to nineteen thousand shares on a typical day. And a stop 6.74 percent away on such a stock can be jumped over by a gap on a bad day. Your sixty-five shares are less than half a percent of a typical day’s volume, so you can get in without moving the price. Getting out is the harder part, which is why I treat the stop as an alert I review daily, not an order I forget. You have ₹5,74,582 in cash, 13.4 percent of net worth. Even the full starter uses less than a quarter of it. You can afford to be patient.

book_subsections.title: The promoter merger: a footnote that is not yet a footnote
paragraphs: There is a corporate item sitting in the margin of this story, and I want you to look at it before you decide it is boring. The company’s promoter is a holding company, ADI BPO Services, which owns 68.34% of MPS. The two are merging. ADI BPO’s MPS shares will be cancelled and the same number issued to ADI BPO’s own shareholders. MPS says this does not dilute you: the public keeps 54,15,201 shares, 31.66% of the register, and the equity meeting approved the scheme, with the public non-institutional holders voting 1,52,327 for and 50 against.

What I would verify, in order: whether the court has given its final sanction (a hearing was listed for 4 November and I could not find the result; the headline that says the tribunal “approves” the merger describes the earlier, procedural step), the exact share-swap ratio and the valuation and fairness reports that sit on the company’s website, whether anything other than the MPS stake comes across, and who the ADI BPO shareholders are.

Why the last one matters to a buyer: today one holding company owns that block. After the merger, ADI BPO’s own shareholders own MPS shares directly. If some of them sold, even one percent of MPS is about a hundred and seventy-one thousand shares, nearly twelve days of a typical day’s volume. I am not predicting a sale. I am telling you that this is the sort of overhang that shows up after a price has been paid, which is one more reason to start with half a position.

book_subsections.title: If I had to explain this to a friend
paragraphs: Imagine we are having coffee and a friend asks whether she should buy MPS. I would say: it is a very good business that I would be glad to own, and I would not buy it today. It has been around for fifty-six years, does the unglamorous work of getting research papers and textbooks ready for the biggest publishers, makes about as much cash as it makes profit, and has no debt. The newest quarter was its strongest ever.

But the shares have already run, then fallen, and they are now in a weak patch. At today’s price I would be risking far more than I could make. If it came back to around ₹2,070, where the 200-day average line is, I would be risking ₹65 to make ₹340 on a generous forecast and ₹171 on a stricter one. That is a deal. A little higher, at ₹2,150, the deal only works if the next quarter’s numbers lift the forecast first.

And I would not put in more than half of my normal amount at first, because this stock has dropped by more than half three times, and its biggest risk is not that the business breaks but that customers who watch AI make production cheaper ask for a lower price at the next big renewal. That is the thing I might be wrong about. If I am wrong in one direction, I miss the first ten percent of a rally. If I am wrong in the other, I avoid a bad trade. I will take that bargain, and I will keep the cash ready.
